newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan restricts protesters to avert islands row.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan restricts protesters to avert islands row.

text.p: Taiwan, seeking to prevent escalation of a sovereignty row over disputed islands in the East China Sea, said on Sunday fishermen who leased boats to activists for a protest voyage to the islands faced punishment.

A protest flotilla involving more than 200 activists and reporters was scheduled to leave Taiwan's northern Shenao port at 10.00 p.m. (1400 GMT) for the disputed Diaoyu archipelago, claimed by Taiwan, Japan and China.
Some 20 activists from Hong Kong were to link up with the flotilla off Taiwan's coast.

The cabinet's Council of Agriculture (COA) told local media that shipowners who rented 16 pleasure boats to the Taiwan activists could have their licences revoked if the vessels go further than 24 nautical miles from Taiwan's shores.

Under Taiwan regulations, fishing boats were not allowed to ferry non-fishermen and pleasure boats are forbidden to sail beyond 24 nautical miles off Taiwan's shores -- far short of the disputed islands.
The Diaoyu archipelago, known in Japanese as the Senkaku islands, lies 200 km (125 miles) northeast of Taiwan.
The Hong Kong activists were held up on Sunday when they put into the central Taiwan port of Taichung to seek medical treatment for an activist hurt in a fall when the boat encountered rough seas.
The activists planned to proceed once doctors decided whether or not the injured man could continue, Hong Kong radio said.
COA officials, who had reportedly asked fishermen not to lease the boats to the activists, said the request was made in the interests of safety, local newspapers reported.
Interior Minister Yeh Chin-fong urged protesters to stay calm, but said maritime police will on hand to help in the event of an emergency.
Hong Kong activist David Chan drowned last September when he jumped from a protest boat into stormy waters near the islands to press China's claim.
"Being emotional cannot solve the problem," Yeh was quoted as saying.
The activists have said they would not rule out landing on the Diaoyus during what they called a "fishing competition" near the islands.
Their "Diaoyu Island World Cup Fishing Contest" was intended to challenge Japan's sovereignty claim by entering into the Japan-claimed waters around the islands, they said.

The cluster of uninhabited islands has ignited fiery nationalist passions in Chinese communities in Hong Kong and Taiwan since a Japanese right-wing group built a makeshift lighthouse there in July 1996.
That action drew protest flotillas of Taiwanese and Hong Kong activists to the island, including Chan's.

On May 6, Shingo Nishimura, a conservative member of Japan's main opposition New Frontier Party, and three other people landed on the islands to inspect security and hold a brief commemorative ceremony, triggering the latest protest.
China's Foreign Ministry has expressed its "strong indignation and opposition", calling the landing a serious violation of China's territorial sovereignty.
Japan took the islands as war booty after defeating imperial China in 1895 and refuses to acknowledge that the dispute is open for discussion with China or Taiwan.
China and Taiwan say the islands have been Chinese territory for centuries and should have been returned after Japan's defeat in World War Two.
